checkpoints: A resumable upload protocol like tus allows a client to pause and resume a transfer hours or even days after creation, so any auth check performed only when the upload is created captures a token whose validity has nothing to do with when the resume actually happens.

Guarding only the POST (creation) handler while leaving PATCH and HEAD unguarded means the resume path — which is the entire point of resumable uploads — has no authentication at all, letting anyone who knows the upload id push chunks or probe its state.

Simply reusing the creation-time token on later PATCH/HEAD requests does not fix the gap either: by the time a real resume happens, hours or days later, that token is very likely expired, so the guard would just reject every genuine resume with a 401.

The correct fix is to require fresh authentication on every state-mutating request (and any request that can leak upload existence or offset), checked against a token supplied per-request, paired with a refresh path the client can call before resuming.

Wiring a tus handler in as a normal NestJS @Controller route means it runs through the exact same request pipeline as every other endpoint, including any global body parser (such as bodyParser.json()) registered in main.ts ahead of all controllers.

A tus PATCH request carries Content-Type: application/offset+octet-stream — a raw binary chunk, not JSON — so routing it through a JSON body-parsing pipeline before the tus handler sees it can silently truncate or corrupt the byte stream.

The structural fix is to register the tus server as raw middleware (e.g. NestMiddleware with RequestMethod.ALL) mounted ahead of the framework's controller pipeline on both the collection path and the per-upload path, so the untouched request and response reach the tus handler before any body parser runs, with the auth check placed inside that same middleware so it applies to every verb.

A demo can pass cleanly while both structural flaws remain invisible: a short test upload finishes in seconds, well inside the token's lifetime, and a small or simple payload can pass through the parsing pipeline without visibly breaking — neither bug surfaces until a real, long-lived, multi-chunk resume is exercised.

Verifying the fix requires two targeted tests: one that lets the token expire mid-upload and asserts the resumed request is freshly re-authenticated rather than silently succeeding or always failing, and one that asserts the stored file is byte-for-byte identical to the source after a multi-chunk upload, which would fail if any parsing step had touched the stream.
